extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying introductory discrete mathematics / mathematical logic
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and solution-strategies for introductory discrete math problems (propositional logic, proofs, counting, number theory). Shows methods (truth tables, DeMorgan, contrapositive, counting principles) and example computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a complete truth table for a propositional formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a truth table for the formula (examples: P ∨ (Q ⇒ R); (P ∧ ∼P) ∨ Q; ∼(P ⇒ Q); (P ∧ ∼P) ⇒ Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include columns for the atomic propositions and for each intermediate subformula, enumerate all 2^n rows of truth-value combinations, and compute the final column. Example rows are shown for all eight combinations of P,Q,R. Use these tables to evaluate formulas (tautology, contradiction, contingent) or to compute resulting truth values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show logical equivalence using truth tables (matching columns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use truth tables to show that two statements are logically equivalent by demonstrating that their truth-value columns agree for every assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute columns for both sides (including intermediate subexpressions). If the columns for the two full formulas are identical across all rows, conclude 'thus since their columns agree, the two statements are logically equivalent.' Example: P ∧ (Q ∨ R) = (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite implication as disjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the equivalence P ⇒ Q = (∼P) ∨ Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this identity to simplify expressions or construct truth tables. The text shows a truth-table verification of P ⇒ Q = (∼P) ∨ Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply DeMorgan's laws and double negation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use DeMorgan's law (for example ∼(∼P ∨ ∼Q) = P ∧ Q) and double-negation transformations to simplify or reason about formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these equivalences when translating, negating, or simplifying logical formulas; the solutions explicitly invoke DeMorgan to show equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate English sentences into symbolic logic with quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Express English statements using predicates, quantifiers (∀, ∃) and logical connectives (examples include universal/existential assertions, 'for every real number x, x^2 > 0', or 'There exists a real number a for which a + x = x for every real x').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the universe, predicate(s), and the correct order of quantifiers; supply predicate names (e.g., P: f is a polynomial) and then build the symbolic form. Include domain restrictions and any necessary side conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negate quantified statements correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Negate sentences involving quantifiers by switching ∀ and ∃ and negating the predicate (example: negate ∀ε ∈ (0,∞) ∃M ... leads to ∃ε ∈ (0,∞) ∀M ... ∃x ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work inside-out: ¬(∀x P(x)) = ∃x ¬P(x), ¬(∃x P(x)) = ∀x ¬P(x); also negate conditional statements appropriately (¬(A ⇒ B) = A ∧ ¬B). The solutions demonstrate the full stepwise negation for epsilon-delta style statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use biconditional reasoning to deduce component truth-values
rubrics_metrics.description: If (R ⇒ S) ⇔ (P ∧ Q) is true and P is known false, deduce the truth-values of R and S without a full truth table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe that if the biconditional is true while one side is false, the other side must be false; for (R ⇒ S) to be false requires R true and S false. The solution gives this pattern as an example of deduction without enumerating all rows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If A then B', sometimes prove the contrapositive 'If not B then not A' (examples: 'If n^2 is even, then n is even' and other contrapositive proofs shown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the contrapositive clearly and prove it; this method is used repeatedly in the solutions. Label intermediate definitions (even = 2k, etc.) and conclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired conclusion and derive a logical contradiction (examples: irrationality proofs for √2, √3; showing no integers a,b with 18a+6b=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the opposite, derive an impossible parity/divisibility conclusion (e.g., both numerator and denominator even), then conclude the original statement. The solutions present standard contradiction proofs for irrationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct proof and algebraic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements directly by starting from hypotheses and performing algebraic manipulations (examples: proving evenness of expressions, divisibility relations like a^2 | b implies a|b in squared form, or ac | bd given a|b and c|d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly introduce integer witnesses (e.g., a = 2c, b = ax) and manipulate equations to reach the conclusion; show existence of integer factors to satisfy divisibility definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by cases when parity or other discrete alternatives occur
rubrics_metrics.description: Split into exhaustive cases (e.g., n even or odd) and prove the claim in each case separately (examples: showing n^2+3n+4 even for all n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate all mutually exclusive possibilities that cover the hypothesis, handle each case with appropriate substitutions (even: n=2a, odd: n=2a+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the multiplication principle for counting (product rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count sequences/lists by multiplying the number of choices at each step (examples: lists of letters with repetition allowed, binary strings, card line-ups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the construction stepwise and multiply choices per position; when restrictions apply (no repetition, fixed positions), adjust counts accordingly. Examples include 6·6·6·6 for 4-letter lists from 6 letters, and 26·25·25·25 for 4-letter codes with no two consecutive equal letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inclusion–exclusion for unions of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute |A ∪ B| or |A ∪ B ∪ C| using inclusion–exclusion: |A|+|B|−|A∩B| (and extend for three sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the event into component sets, compute sizes of singletons and intersections, then apply the formula. Examples include counting 4-digit integers that are even or contain no zeros, and counting 7-digit binary strings with several overlapping properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count combinations/permutations with and without repetition; use binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Use n!/(k!(n−k)!) and other combinatorial formulas to count subsets, placements, and codes (examples: number of 10-element subsets from 37-element set, 16-digit binary strings with seven 1's).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate model (ordered vs unordered, repetition allowed vs not) and compute using factorials or binomial coefficients; the text gives many numeric examples and answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the binomial theorem to derive coefficients and combinatorial identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use (x+y)^n expansion to obtain coefficients (e.g., coefficient of x^8 in (x+2)^13) and to prove identities by evaluating at special values (e.g., set y=1 or y=−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the desired term's binomial coefficient and plug in numeric values for variables if necessary; use substitutions (1+1)^n, (1+(−1))^n, (10+(−1))^n) to derive summation identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factorization and algebraic identities in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor expressions (e.g., x^2 − y^2 = (x − y)(x + y)) to reduce problems and allow division by nonzero factors when justified (example: from (x−y)(x+y)=5(x−y) deduce x+y=5 if x−y≠0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform factoring steps explicitly and consider case when a factor is zero (handle separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply definitions of even, odd, divisibility in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the standard definitions: even means 2k, odd means 2k+1, divisibility a|b means b = a·k, and use these to construct integer witnesses in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute these canonical forms to transform statements about parity or divisibility into algebraic equalities, then reason about parity/divisibility of resulting expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use congruence/modular arithmetic properties for algebraic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use n | (a−b) to deduce congruences (a ≡ b (mod n)) and propagate congruences through algebraic operations (if a ≡ b (mod n) then a^3 ≡ b^3 (mod n); multiply congruence by c to get ca ≡ cb (mod n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate by writing a−b = nc and multiplying or factoring as needed; use the division algorithm/gcd properties when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the division algorithm and gcd identities in number-theory proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a = q b + r, then gcd(a,b) = gcd(r,b); also use gcd properties like gcd(a,b) = gcd(a−b,b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the division algorithm to reduce gcd computations and provide direct divisibility arguments; the solutions include standard Euclidean algorithm steps and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing/complement argument to show parity of combinatorial counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Show an even number of combinatorial objects by pairing each object with a distinct complement (example: for a set A with 2n elements, each n-element subset X pairs with its complement, so C(2n,n) is even).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an involution with no fixed points (X ↔ complement X) to partition the set into pairs, yielding an even total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason about primes dividing factorials/binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Use factorization of p! and compare prime factors to argue that a prime p divides certain binomial coefficients (example: if p is prime and 0
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe that p appears in prime factorization of p! but not in k! or (p−k)!, hence must divide C(p,k). The textbook uses this argument to show divisibility by primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret natural-language connectives carefully (e.g., 'but' as 'and')
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating English to logic, interpret rhetorical connectives in standard logical terms; the text notes 'The “but” can be interpreted as “and.”' when negating or translating sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about intended logical meaning; do not assume extra logical content in colloquial connectors beyond their logical equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose counting problems into disjoint types and multiply within types
rubrics_metrics.description: Break combinatorial objects into disjoint forms/types (e.g., positions where a pair of vowels occurs) and count each type using multiplication principle, then sum results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure types are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive; multiply choices for each position within a type and then add counts across types. Example: counting 6-letter lists with two consecutive vowels by considering the five possible positions for the vowel pair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negate conditional statements correctly when forming counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the equivalence ¬(A ⇒ B) = A ∧ ¬B to find witnesses when negating conditional statements (used in negating epsilon-delta statements and other conditionals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When negating implications inside quantified formulas, apply implication negation after switching quantifiers appropriately; the solutions show the transformation step-by-step for complex negations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity and divisibility arguments iteratively to reach contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: In contradiction proofs about rationality or divisibility, repeatedly deduce divisibility of numerator and denominator by the same prime to derive a contradiction (example: assume a/b reduced for √3 and deduce 3|a and 3|b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that a prime dividing a^2 implies it divides a (prove as a sub-lemma by checking remainders), then apply to both numerator and denominator to contradict reduction assumption.
